title: Grocery shopping: quantities
topic: quantities, weights, containers; asking and paying
why: After hay and está, this lesson takes you to the market: quantities, weights and containers, how Spanish handles “some,” and the phrases for ordering and paying (me pone, ¿algo más?, ¿cuánto es?). It recycles numbers, prices and present-tense irregulars, and sets you up for the restaurant lesson.

Un kilo de, una botella de…

For quantities, Spanish works like English: quantity + de (“of”) + product, with no article. Un kilo de tomates, just like “a kilo of tomatoes.”

SpanishEnglish
un kilo de naranjasa kilo of oranges
medio kilo de fresashalf a kilo of strawberries
un kilo y medio de patatasa kilo and a half of potatoes
un cuarto de kilo de quesoa quarter kilo of cheese
cien gramos de jamóna hundred grams of ham
una docena de huevosa dozen eggs
una botella de aceitea bottle of oil
una lata de atúna can of tuna
un paquete de arroza package of rice
un litro de lechea liter of milk

Medio: no article

“Half a kilo” is medio kilo, with no un in front (never “a half kilo” word for word). And medio agrees in gender: media docena (half a dozen), media botella. After a number, it goes at the end, just like English “and a half”: un kilo y medio, una hora y media. Notice too that English says “a dozen eggs” with no “of,” while Spanish always needs its “of” there too.

Cien gramos: before a noun, 100 is always cien, never “ciento.” You saw this with numbers.

Medio kilo de tomates y una docena de huevos, por favor.Half a kilo of tomatoes and a dozen eggs, please.
", "

No word for “some” here

When English says “some” or “any” for an unspecified amount, Spanish usually says nothing at all: just the bare noun. Don't try to translate “some bread” or “any water.”

EnglishSpanish
I want some bread.Quiero pan.
Do you have any water?¿Tienes agua?
I'm buying some apples.Compro manzanas.
There's no milk.No hay leche.

Un poco de, algo de, nada de

SpanishEnglishExample
un poco dea little, a bit ofUn poco de queso, por favor.
algo desome, something to¿Quieres algo de beber? (would you like something to drink?)
mucho, muchaa lot of, much, manyHay mucha fruta. (no de!)
nada deno… at allNo hay nada de pan. (there's no bread at all)

Careful: “a lot of” is mucho with no de, and as you already know, mucho agrees with its noun: muchas naranjas.

No… nada: Spanish uses a double negative, which standard English avoids. No quiero nada = I don't want anything (literally “I don't want nothing”), and in Spanish that's perfectly correct. On its own, Nada más means “nothing else.”

¿Tienes leche? No, no hay nada de leche.Do you have any milk? No, there's no milk at all.
", "

At the market: ordering and paying

At the market or the corner store, the exchange almost always follows the same pattern. Here are the lines, for the customer and the vendor:

WhoSpanishEnglish
customer¿Quién es el último?Who's last? (to find your place in line)
vendor¿Qué quería?What can I get you?
customerMe pone un kilo de tomates, por favor.Could I have a kilo of tomatoes, please?
customer¿Cuánto cuestan las fresas?How much are the strawberries?
vendorAquí tiene. ¿Algo más?Here you go. Anything else?
customerSí, también quería una docena de huevos.Yes, I'd also like a dozen eggs.
customerNo, nada más, gracias. ¿Cuánto es?No, nothing else, thanks. How much is that?
vendorSon ocho euros con cincuenta.That's eight euros fifty.
vendor¿Con tarjeta o en efectivo?Card or cash?

Me pone…: the shop phrase

Me pone comes from poner (to put), in the polite usted form. Literally, “you put me…” It's the most natural way to order in a shop in Spain, and it doesn't sound rude at all, even without a “could you”: learn it as it is. Quería… (I'd like…) works very well too.

At a Spanish market, there isn't always a visible line: when you arrive, you ask ¿Quién es el último? (or ¿Quién es la última?), and you go after that person.

For prices: ocho euros con cincuenta, or simply ocho cincuenta (€8.50).
